title: Take the 150-level combinational divider off the EX path: stall-based radix-2 iterative DIV/REM unit + one shared 33x33 signed multiplier
motivation:
The baseline runs at 5.44 MHz. Its worst path (199.8 ns, 150 logic levels,
156 cells) runs MEM/WB.rd -> u_fwd -> u_ex -> u_ex/u_alu -> EX/MEM.alu_result
(absorbed into the dmem BSRAM address register). The only thing in alu.sv that
can be 150 levels deep is the combinational 32-bit `/` and `%` array (DIV/DIVU/
REM/REMU plus their signed variants, all built in parallel). Every other path in
the core (forward mux + 32-bit add/compare, and the DSP multiplier) is roughly
an order of magnitude shorter. Checked on the built coremark.elf with objdump:
the only div/divu/rem/remu instructions are 5 `divu` in main (result
reporting), plus `mulhu` divide-by-constant sequences in core_list_init and
ee_printf. None of them are in the timed kernels. matrix_* uses only `mul`,
and list/state/crc use no M-extension ops at all. So making division
slow costs essentially no IPC, while removing it from the single-cycle EX path
should raise Fmax several-fold. Fitness = IPC x Fmax, so this is by far the
largest single lever available. No other micro-opt can pay off until this path
is gone. test_alu.py notes a multi-cycle divider existed in an earlier
iteration (hyp-20260427-002) and was reverted during the v2 reset, not because
it failed.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational divider with a sequential radix-2 restoring divider
that stalls the front of the pipeline while it runs. In the same change,
collapse the three 32x32 multipliers into one shared 33x33 signed multiply, so
the new critical path (forward mux -> multiplier -> result mux) is as short as
possible.

1. New module rtl/divider.sv (clocked, has reset). Ports: start, op (DIV/DIVU/
   REM/REMU), a, b (the post-forward rs1/rs2), busy, done, result.
   - Cycle 0 (start): register the raw operands, the op, sign flags
     (a_neg = signed_op & a[31], b_neg = signed_op & b[31]) and b_is_zero.
     Keep the forwarding mux -> abs() -> register path out of the start
     cycle: take abs() from the *registered* operands on the next cycle,
     so the only logic on the forwarding path is a register capture.
   - 32 iterations of a 33-bit trial subtract with a remainder/quotient
     shift register. Each iteration is about one 33-bit carry chain plus a
     2:1 mux, far below the EX ALU add path.
   - Final cycle: quotient = b_is_zero ? 32'hFFFFFFFF
                              : (a_neg ^ b_neg ? -q : q);
                  remainder = a_neg ? -r : r   (b==0 then gives r = |a|,
                  and negating yields a, as required).
     INT_MIN / -1 falls out naturally: |INT_MIN| = 0x80000000, q stays
     0x80000000 because the signs match, and r = 0. Register the selected
     32-bit result so EX/MEM is loaded from a flop, not from a negate
     chain.
   - `done` stays high until the EX/MEM register actually captures the
     result (i.e. until !stall_ex_mem). This covers a dmem stall that
     overlaps the end of the divide. `done` clears on that same edge, so a
     back-to-back DIV entering ID/EX on that edge starts cleanly next cycle.
   - Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`: same FSM and handshake, but the
     iteration count is shortened to 2 and the result is the ALTOPS formula
     from alu.sv ((a - b) ^ const per op) computed on the latched operands.
     This keeps the stall/hold/bubble logic under formal checking while
     staying well inside the depth-20 liveness/insn BMC bound.
2. rtl/alu.sv: delete the four `/` and `%` arms, so the combinational ALU has
   no divider at all. Replace mul_ss/mul_uu/mul_su with one product:
     a_ext = {a[31] & (op==MULH || op==MULHSU), a}
     b_ext = {b[31] & (op==MULH), b}
     prod  = $signed(a_ext) * $signed(b_ext)   (66-bit; use [63:0])
     MUL -> prod[31:0]; MULH/MULHSU/MULHU -> prod[63:32].
   The two sign-extension bits come from the decoded op only; they do not
   depend on data. This drops from 3 products (6 DSPs today) to one
   36x36-class DSP mapping and removes a 3-way product-select level from
   the result mux. Keep the ALTOPS arms for MUL* unchanged.
3. rtl/ex_stage.sv: instantiate divider. is_div = in.valid &&
   alu_op in {DIV,DIVU,REM,REMU}. Start the divider when is_div && !busy &&
   !done. Output div_stall = is_div && !done to the top level. While
   div_stall is high and EX/MEM is not dmem-stalled, EX/MEM captures a
   bubble: valid=0 and the whole ctrl cleared, so reg_write=0 and
   mem_read=mem_write=0, and the forward unit and dmem see nothing. When
   done, EX/MEM captures the divider result as alu_result. Its rs1_val/
   rs2_val (RVFI only) must come from the divider's latched operands, not
   the live forward mux. While EX is stalled, the producers ahead retire
   out of EX/MEM and MEM/WB, so the forward mux would otherwise fall back
   to the stale ID/EX regfile copy.
4. rtl/hazard_unit.sv + rtl/core.sv: add a div_stall input. stall_if |=
   div_stall, stall_id |= div_stall (hold ID/EX, do not bubble it).
   flush_id is unchanged: while a DIV sits in EX, redirect=0 and
   id_ex_mem_read=0, so neither a load-use nor a redirect can kill the DIV.
   Redirect keeps its priority over stall in if_stage exactly as today.
Expected result: the 150-level path disappears. The new worst path should be
MEM/WB.rd -> forward-select -> operand mux -> DSP multiply (or 32-bit
compare -> redirect -> PC) at roughly 25-40 ns, i.e. about 25-40 MHz vs
5.44 MHz. IPC barely moves (~0 divides in the timed region, ~34 cycles
each), so fitness should rise several-fold, far past the +4.6% acceptance
bar. LUT count should also drop sharply: the 12.3k LUTs are mostly the
divider array. That lowers routing congestion, which helps Fmax further.

title: Move M-ext out of the 1-cycle ALU into a multi-cycle mul/div unit that stalls EX
motivation:
The baseline runs at 5.44 MHz. Its worst path is 199.8 ns deep with 150 logic
levels: MEM/WB.rd -> forward_unit -> EX forward mux -> u_alu -> EX/MEM
alu_result -> dmem BSRAM. Gowin folds the EX/MEM address register into the
BSRAM input register, so that is where the path ends. The logic depth comes
from alu.sv evaluating four fully combinational 32-bit dividers (signed and
unsigned `/` and `%`) and three separate 64-bit multipliers every cycle. The
same logic accounts for most of the 12.3k LUT4. Division is almost absent
from the timed CoreMark region, and MUL is only a few percent of the dynamic
instruction mix. The design therefore pays a roughly 10x clock penalty for
operations that are rare. Without the M-ext logic, the longest
paths should be the forward mux -> 32-bit add/compare/shift -> EX/MEM path
and the branch redirect -> PC path, both around 15-25 ns on GW2AR-18.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split the M-extension out of the single-cycle ALU into a new functional unit,
rtl/muldiv.sv, with its own FSM and a stall handshake into the pipeline:

1. alu.sv keeps only the RV32I ops: ADD/SUB/logic/SLT(U)/shifts/LUI. The
   multipliers and dividers are removed. ALU_MUL..ALU_REMU codes stay in
   core_pkg.sv and select the muldiv result.
2. muldiv.sv:
   - Multiplier: a single 33x33 signed product. Extend the operands per op:
     MUL/MULH sign/sign, MULHSU sign/zero, MULHU zero/zero. This replaces the
     three separate 64-bit products and maps to the Gowin DSP.
     The forwarded operands go straight into the multiplier, and the product
     is registered inside muldiv. The result (lo or hi half) comes out of
     that register, so a MUL costs 1 extra EX cycle. If the
     fwd-mux -> DSP -> product-reg path then becomes the critical path in
     `make timing`, also register the operands at start (2 extra cycles).
   - Divider: radix-2 restoring divider, 1 quotient bit per cycle for
     32 cycles, shared by DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU. Operands are captured as
     absolute values at start, and signs are fixed up at the end:
     quotient sign = sa^sb, remainder sign = sa. Unsigned restoring division
     by 0 already returns q=all-ones and r=dividend. The special case is
     signed division by 0: the quotient must not be negated (the spec result
     is -1). INT_MIN/-1 falls out naturally (q=0x80000000, r=0).
   - The unit captures its operands on the first cycle an M-op is in EX.
     At that point the EX forward muxes are valid. The unit must not re-read
     them later, because MEM/WB keeps draining and the forwarding sources go
     stale while EX is held.
   - FSM: IDLE -> BUSY -> DONE. DONE stays set until EX/MEM actually
     captures the result, i.e. a cycle with !stall_ex_mem, so a dmem stall
     that overlaps completion cannot lose the result. The unit then returns
     to IDLE, which lets back-to-back M-ops restart cleanly.
   - Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`, keep the same FSM and stall
     handshake, but return the existing alt formulas computed from the
     captured operands, with a short fixed latency (1-2 cycles for every
     op). This keeps M-op retirement inside the depth-20 BMC window and
     still exercises the stall and forwarding path in formal.
3. Pipeline integration (ex_stage.sv, hazard_unit.sv, core.sv): define
   md_stall = (valid M-op in ID/EX) && !md_done. While md_stall is high:
   - hold the PC (stall_if);
   - hold ID/EX without flushing it (stall_id);
   - write a bubble into EX/MEM (valid=0, reg_write=0, mem_read=0,
     mem_write=0) so older instructions drain through MEM/WB normally.
     Do not freeze EX/MEM: a held store would repeat its UART/MMIO write.
   When md_done is set, EX/MEM captures the muldiv result in place of
   alu_result. dmem_stall keeps its current priority over everything.
   An M-op in EX is never a redirect source, and it is never flushed while
   it sits in EX, so the unit needs no kill input.
4. Add a decoder/ctrl bit `is_muldiv` (valid only for funct7=0000001 OP),
   or derive it from the alu_op range. Invariant 10 is unaffected: is_illegal
   defaults are unchanged.

Expected result: Fmax rises from 5.4 MHz to roughly 40-70 MHz, and LUT use
drops sharply because four dividers and two of the three multipliers go
away. CoreMark cycles grow by about 3-6% (MUL +1 cycle, DIV ~+33 cycles but
nearly absent in the timed region). Net fitness should be several times the
current 12.12. The schema caps the estimate at +50.

title: Fetch-time branch prediction: 64-entry bimodal BHT + same-cycle predecoded JAL/branch targets
motivation:
The core has no IF/ID register: imem_data arrives combinationally in the
same cycle the PC is presented and is decoded that same cycle. Every
taken branch / JAL / JALR resolves in EX and costs one flushed fetch
slot (flush_if + flush_id), regardless of istall (the slot is wasted
whether or not imem was ready), so each avoided redirect saves exactly
one cycle.
Measured with test/cosim/reference.py on the canonical CoreMark build
(-O3, 2K, between the 0x10000100/0x10000104 markers, 10 iterations,
2.92M instructions):
  - conditional branches 529.6k (18.1% of instrs), 55.6% taken
  - JAL 49.4k, JALR 13.7k (all returns)
  - taken control flow = 357.5k = 12.2% of instructions -> 35.7k
    redirect bubbles per iteration out of ~449k cycles/iteration
    (449k = 5.442 MHz / 12.12 iter/s), i.e. ~8% of all cycles.
Predictor accuracy on the same trace (branch mispredicts / 10 iters):
  BTFN 111.2k; bimodal 2-bit 16e 70.4k, 32e 55.6k, 64e 51.8k,
  128e 54.5k, 256e 44.3k; gshare is worse at every size tried
  (64e/4b-hist 64.5k, 256e/8b 55.6k). A 4-entry RAS would catch all
  13.7k returns but that is only ~0.3% of cycles, not worth adding a
  32-bit JALR target compare, so JALR stays unpredicted.
Fmax is pinned at 5.44 MHz by the combinational divider (199 ns path
fwd->alu->EX/MEM). In fpga/core_bench_si.sv io_imemData comes from a
registered LFSR, so the new fetch loop (imem_data -> predecode -> 32b
add -> PC mux -> PC reg) is a short reg-to-reg path that cannot become
critical. Nearly all of the IPC gain turns into fitness.

Predict direction and compute the target at fetch time. There is no
BTB: the fetched instruction is visible in the same cycle as its PC, so
the target is pc + imm straight from imem_data.

if_stage.sv:

    (weakly not-taken); read index = pc[7:2] (PC register, so the read
    is off a flop).
  * predecode imem_data: f_jal = opcode==1101111; f_br = opcode==1100011
    && funct3 not in {2,3}; f_imm = J-imm or B-imm; f_tgt = pc + f_imm.
  * pred_taken = !flush && !redirect && (f_jal || (f_br && bht[idx][1]))
    && f_imm[1]==0 (never predict to a misaligned target, so the
    existing EX misalign-trap path is untouched: such instructions go
    down the pred_taken=0 path exactly as today).

compare -> flush/stall combine -> RESET pin of all ID/EX rs?_val flops

title: Registered IF/ID stage fetched from the next-PC mux: break the redirect -> IF NOP-mux -> regfile-address / load-use -> ID/EX-hold loop
motivation:
`make timing TARGET=bench` on the current champion (hyp-20260929-001, 49.3 MHz)
shows every top path is the same 27.2 ns, 20-level chain:
  cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s0 (Gowin mapped the regfile into a BSRAM and folded
  the ID/EX rs*_val flops into it, so DO is the effective ID/EX rs2_val, tC2Q
  2.26 ns)
  -> ID/EX hold/bypass mux -> alu_b / forward mux -> 32-bit branch comparator
     carry chain (u_ex n303..n327)
  -> branch_cond / redirect (u_ex n1139)
  -> u_if n69 (out.instr = (flush||redirect) ? NOP : imem_data, fanout 102)
  -> u_if rs2_addr_w (the regfile read address is taken from that muxed instr)
  -> u_hazard load-use 5-bit compare (carry chain n12..n14)
  -> u_id stall/flush -> ID/EX rs2_val hold mux (fanout 33) -> FF.
Path 5 ends at u_if/pc via the same chain. The cause is the design's
*combinational* IF/ID: the EX-stage redirect is ANDed into the
instruction word that drives the decoder, the regfile read address and the
load-use detector, and then back into the ID/EX enable. So one cycle holds
branch-resolve + fetch-kill + register-read addressing + hazard + stall
distribution. The multiplier is not on the path and the divider is gone
(see LESSONS), so this loop alone sets Fmax.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make IF a real pipeline stage with a registered IF/ID {pc, instr, valid} and
drive the instruction bus from the next-fetch-address mux, as a sync-BRAM
fetch would:
  imem_addr = redirect ? redirect_target : fetch_pc_q
On each edge where IF/ID is not held (or on any redirect), IF/ID captures
{imem_addr, imem_data, imem_ready}, and fetch_pc_q <= imem_ready ?
imem_addr + 4 : imem_addr. An invalid capture (imem stall) loads NOP
0x00000013 with valid=0, so the decoder, the regfile address and the hazard
unit never see a wrong-path rs field. They no longer need the
(flush||redirect) mux either.
Why IPC is unchanged: a taken branch/jump in EX fetches its target in the
same cycle (imem_addr is combinational from the redirect mux), and IF/ID
holds the target at the next edge. So the redirect penalty stays at 1
bubble, as today. Load-use stays at 1 bubble. An imem stall still costs 1
slot. Cosim is safe: main.cpp samples io_imemAddr after the previous
posedge eval, and redirect depends only on flops (ID/EX, EX/MEM.alu_result,
MEM/WB). imem_addr must NOT depend on io_imemReady/io_dmemReady. In the
timed netlist imem_addr feeds only the LED XOR, an unconstrained output,
so redirect->imem_addr adds no reg-to-reg path.

ID/EX. Compare IF/ID.rs1/rs2 against ID/EX.rd (becomes EX/MEM next cycle
-> sel 1) and EX/MEM.rd (becomes MEM/WB -> sel 2). Keep EX/MEM priority,
x0 excluded and reg_write gating. ID/EX only advances when EX/MEM and
MEM/WB also advance: a dmem stall holds ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB data
together, and a div stall holds ID/EX while the divider has already latched
its operands. So selects registered at capture stay valid while ID/EX is
held. The regfile's write-first bypass keeps covering the WB write in the

title: Operand/result path micro-opts: LUT-RAM regfile, registered one-hot fwd selects, DSP product merged at last result LUT
motivation:
Measured with `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (57.7 MHz; data
path 17.3 ns = 22.628 ns arrival - 5.33 ns clock insertion):
ALL of the top-25 setup paths start at `cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s`. Gowin
has mapped the 32x32 regfile to BSRAM with a synchronous read, absorbing
the ID/EX rs?_val flops. Every EX path therefore starts with the BSRAM
tC2Q (2.26 ns, vs 0.2-0.4 ns for a fabric FF). Two LUT levels follow in
u_id: the write-first bypass plus the `regs_ER_RS` masking that Gowin
emulates for the RTL's reset-all-32-registers loop.
Path 1 then runs fwd mux (3 LUTs) -> 33x33 DSP (3.76 ns, DOUT[32] = MULH
bit) -> SIX LUT levels of the one-hot result AND-OR (`ex_result_0_s64 ->
s47 -> s29 -> s14 -> s4 -> s0`, about 4.7 ns). Synthesis put the
latest-arriving net (the DSP output) at the HEAD of the OR chain.
PROTOTYPED IN THIS SESSION: removing the reset loop (initial zero-fill
instead) and adding `syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram"` does move the
regfile to LUT-RAM (LUT-RAM 8 -> 32, BSRAM 6 -> 4, 2387 LUT). But Fmax only
reaches 60.38 MHz (+4.6%) because the next path is almost as long:
`u_mem/reg_q.rd` / `u_ex/data_q.rd` -> u_fwd equality compare (a carry
chain, about 1.4 ns plus routing) -> fwd mux -> DSP -> the same six-level
result OR (16.3 ns), and the same compare -> branch compare -> redirect ->
PC CE (16.3 ns). So the regfile fix needs the other two fixes too. This
also explains why round 2's redirect-loop rewrites (002-r2s1, 003-r2s2)
gained nothing: the BSRAM-regfile start point bounded every path.

(IPC and cycle count unchanged at 4.49M; cosim/formal semantics unchanged):

unused; keep it with a lint waiver. EX paths then start at a fabric FF with
no ID-side LUTs.

ID, in parallel with the regfile read, and register it in ID/EX next to

  fwd1_exmem_next = id_ex.reg_write && id_ex.rd!=0 && id_ex.rd==if_id.rs1

title: Fetch-time bimodal+JAL predictor rebased on the 001-r2s0 champion, with a flop-selected redirect target
motivation:
The champion (hyp-20260929-001-r2s0, 57.824 MHz, 4,491,817 cycles, 128.73)
runs the same cycles as the baseline: every taken branch, JAL and JALR
resolves in EX and costs one flushed fetch slot. That is 357.5k bubbles per
10 iterations, about 8% of all cycles (reference.py trace: 529.6k
conditional branches, 55.6% taken; 49.4k JAL; 13.7k JALR).
Fetch-time prediction has already been measured twice. In both runs the
IPC gain was real and the lost fitness came from the base it was built on:
  - 003-r1s2 (same-cycle, 1-cycle mispredict recovery, 64-entry bimodal +
    JAL) measured 4,201,766 cycles, -6.45% vs 4,491,485. It sat on the
    5.4 MHz divider-bound core, so the gain was lost there.
  - 003-r2s2 (mispredict registered in EX/MEM, 2-cycle recovery) measured
    4,265,800 cycles. It sat on 001-r1s0 and missed 001-r2s0's ctrl-only
    flush and one-hot result mux, so its Fmax stayed around 50 MHz.

IPC win and do not expect it to raise Fmax. The one condition is that it
must not add logic levels to the champion's paths. Those are the
regfile->fwd->ALU->EX/MEM.alu_result path at 22.6 ns, and the redirect
path branch compare -> redirect -> PC mux / ctrl-only flush_id right
behind it.

only feeds the LED XOR. So the new fetch loop (imem_data -> predecode ->
pc+imm -> PC mux -> PC) is a short reg-to-reg path of about 10 ns,
against a 17.3 ns period.

Use the 1-cycle-recovery design (003-r1s2, the better of the two IPC
results) on top of the champion. Add three timing-motivated changes so the
EX redirect path and the ALU path gain no LUT levels.

Fetch (if_stage.sv):
  * bht: 64 x 2-bit saturating counters in flops, reset to 2'b01. The read
    index is pc[7:2], taken straight off the PC register.
  * Predecode the raw same-cycle imem_data:
      f_jal = opcode==1101111
      f_br  = opcode==1100011 && funct3 not in {2,3}
      f_imm = instr[3] ? J-imm : B-imm   (one mux level)
      f_tgt = pc + f_imm                 (one 32-bit adder)
    pred_taken = (f_jal || (f_br && bht[idx][1])) && !f_imm[1]. A target
    that would be misaligned is never predicted, so the existing EX
    misalign trap path is untouched.
  * PC priority: reset > redirect > stall (hold) > pred_taken ? f_tgt :
    pc+4. PC advances through the fetch path exactly when
    !stall_if && !redirect, and that is exactly when ID/EX captures a
    valid instruction (stall_id=0, flush_id=0). So the prediction latched
    into ID/EX is always the one that steered the PC. The no-NOP-mux
    raw-word convention from 001-r2s0 stays.
  * Export pred_taken and the 2-bit counter value (bht_ctr) in if_id_t.
  * BHT write port driven only from EX/MEM flops:
      en    = ex_mem.valid && ex_mem.ctrl.is_branch
      idx   = ex_mem.pc[7:2]
      taken = ex_mem.branch_taken
      new   = sat(ex_mem.bht_ctr, taken)
    A branch is never held in EX/MEM (dmem_stall needs a mem op there), so
    each branch updates exactly once. Keeping the update off the EX compare
    matters: the compare must not fan out to 128 BHT flop enables.

flops with no reset or flush. They are only read through is_branch and
is_jump, which are already in the sync-cleared ctrl group, so a bubble can
never redirect. The flush fanout stays at 6 flops.

  * redirect = pred_taken_q ? (is_branch && !branch_cond)
                            : ((branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault)
    Everything except branch_cond comes from flops or is early, so the
    late compare still reaches redirect through one LUT.
    - A predicted JAL never redirects: its target is the same pc+imm and
      it cannot be misaligned.
    - A predicted-taken branch redirects only when not taken.
    - JALR is never predicted, so it redirects as today.
  * redirect_target = is_jalr ? {addr_sum[31:1],1'b0}
                              : (pred_taken_q ? pc_plus4 : pc_plus_imm)

    The late JALR adder keeps its single final mux level, the same depth
    as today's is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target. The late `actual`
    compare result never selects the target.
  * pc_next, the misalign traps, ctrl_with_trap and all EX/MEM/RVFI
    contents stay architectural and unchanged. Add bht_ctr to EX/MEM
    (branch_taken, pc and ctrl.is_branch are already there).

`redirect`, which now fires only on mispredicts and JALRs.

described. Do not move to the 2-cycle registered-mispredict scheme: it
costs +64k cycles for no measured Fmax gain (003-r2s2).

title: Resolve distance-2 forwarding in ID and pre-decode the branch redirect so every EX operand path starts with a single 2:1 bypass
motivation:
The champion (001-r3s0, 82.47 MHz, 4.49M cycles) is limited by a family of
near-equal EX paths that all begin at the same operand-forwarding mux. The
reported worst path is EX/MEM.alu_result -> rs1/rs2 forward mux -> branch
compare -> redirect -> hazard flush -> ID/EX valid_q (13 logic levels,
18.5 ns arrival incl. clock insertion); its siblings run through the same
forward mux into the ALU/address adder (-> dmem BSRAM address), the DSP
inputs and the JALR target -> PC. Today each EX operand is a 3-source
AND-OR (EX/MEM.alu_result, WB write-data, ID/EX rs?_val) with two select
bits, and the WB source is itself a mux (mem_to_reg ? read_data :
alu_result) of MEM/WB flops, so the operand is 2-3 LUT levels deep before
any arithmetic. Behind the compare, the redirect is a 5-7 input function
of a 3-bit branch_op case over three comparators (eq, signed lt, unsigned
lt), is_branch, is_jump and the pc+imm misalignment bits, which costs
another 2-3 levels before the flush LUT. In the timed bench the fetch word
comes from a flop (LFSR) and the regfile is async LUT-RAM, so the ID stage
has a lot of slack that can absorb work taken off EX. IPC stays the same,
so this is a pure Fmax play on the paths `make timing` actually names.

Measured on the champion (`make timing TARGET=bench`, place option 0,
75.6 MHz, 13.2 ns data delay), the top 5 paths are tied within 0.14 ns:
  1. EX/MEM.alu_result -> valid_q RESET (ID/EX flush), 13.19 ns
  2. ID/EX.fwd2_memwb select -> ALU/DSP -> EX/MEM.alu_result, 13.18 ns
  3/4. EX/MEM.alu_result -> redirect -> PC D / CE pins, 13.17 ns
  5. MEM/WB.ctrl.mem_to_reg -> WB mux -> fwd mux -> ALU -> alu_result,
     13.05 ns
and paths 6-24 are the same redirect family ending on the other kill
flops and PC CE pins. Path 1 cell by cell: 2 LUTs for the operand
forward mux (~2.8 ns incl. routing), the 32-bit compare carry chain
(~1.6 ns), then FIVE LUT levels (~7.4 ns incl. routing: branch_op case
-> branch_taken/misalign -> redirect (fanout 31) -> flush (fanout 6))
into valid_q. Every one of these families starts at the fwd select flops,
the WB mux or the 3-source operand mux, and the redirect family also has
an avoidable 2-3 LUT tail after the compare.

path families (LESSONS: fix every tied family in one iteration):

   (the WB mux disappears; MEM/WB.result drives the regfile write port and
   the write-first bypass straight from a flop), and in id_stage select

   holds a value that is already correct except for the distance-1
   producer, so EX's operand becomes a 2:1 mux:

motivation:

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Change the bypass-network topology so the two older bypass sources are
resolved one cycle earlier, at the ID/EX register input. In EX this
leaves exactly one bypass (EX/MEM -> EX), a single LUT3 of flops.
1. WB data registered in MEM. mem_stage computes wb_next =
   mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result (the old wb_stage mux) and
   registers it as MEM/WB.wdata. The regfile write port and RVFI
   rd_wdata read this flop directly.
2. MEM->EX forwarding moves to ID/EX capture. The instruction that
   will sit in MEM/WB when the ID instruction reaches EX is the one
   now in EX/MEM (ID/EX captures only when !stall_id, and stall_id
   covers dmem_stall and div_stall). So its final result is
   mem_stage's wb_next this cycle: load data is valid whenever
   !dmem_stall. id_stage muxes rs?_val_next = fwd?_ex ? (don't care) :
   fwd?_mem ? wb_next : regfile_read (with the existing WB write-first
   bypass, now fed by a flop). It drops the fwd?_memwb flags.
   Consequence: a held ID/EX already carries the right value, so the
   old MEM/WB hold_wb forwarding is no longer needed for correctness.
3. Immediate folded into rs2_val. For instructions whose ALU b-operand
   is the immediate (OP-IMM, JALR, LUI, AUIPC; alu_src && !mem_write),
   ID loads rs2_val with the (AUIPC-folded) immediate and forces
   fwd2_exmem = 0. Stores and branches keep the real rs2, and the
   address adder / branch target keep using the separate imm field.
   EX then has alu_b = mul_b = rs2 = fwd2_exmem ? EX/MEM.alu_result :

   instructions (or keeps a separate RVFI-only copy, which is pruned
   in synthesis).

alu_src LUT, and the shamt fanout-78 net is driven by one LUT3 of
flops. Path 5 loses the WB mux and one forward LUT, and its start
point becomes the EX/MEM flop. The redirect loop loses one forward
LUT. The ALU, DSP operands and address adder gain the same 1-2 levels.
The new ID-side path (BSRAM dout -> load align -> wb_next mux ->
rs_val mux -> ID/EX) is about 5 LUTs after the BSRAM clock-to-out,

forwarding coverage, same load-use and redirect bubbles, so CoreMark
cycles stay at about 4.49M. Removing about 1.2-1.6 ns from ~13.2 ns
gives about +9-13% Fmax (median about 90-93 MHz), and fitness rises by
the same factor.

redirect loop will likely be the single worst path. Registering the
branch resolution (flop-driven early redirect for JAL/backward
branches, late fix-up from EX/MEM) is the next structural step.

title: Re-apply the measured Fmax-neutral bimodal+JAL fetch predictor (1-cycle recovery, flop-selected redirect) on the 001-r3s0 champion
motivation:
The champion (hyp-20260929-001-r3s0: 82.472 MHz median, 4,491,817 cycles,
183.60) runs baseline cycles. Every taken branch/JAL/JALR resolves in EX
and costs one flushed fetch slot: 357.5k bubbles per run, about 8% of
cycles (529.6k conditional branches, 55.6% taken; 49.4k JAL; 13.7k JALR).

I ran `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (place option 0,
75.6 MHz). The top paths are three tied families within 0.14 ns:
  1. 18.518 ns  EX/MEM.alu_result -> fwd mux -> 32b branch compare chain ->
     4 LUTs (branch_op select / taken / misalign / redirect) -> flush ->
     ID/EX valid_q; the same family also ends at pc[*] and the ID/EX kill
     bits (most of the top 25 paths).
  2. 18.512 ns  ID/EX.fwd2_memwb -> rs2/alu_b -> shamt (fanout 78) ->
     barrel shifter + result OR -> alu_result.
  3. 18.381 ns  MEM/WB.mem_to_reg -> WB mux -> fwd -> ALU -> alu_result.
Because 2 and 3 tie with 1, registering the redirect (the 003-r2s2
scheme: 4,265,800 cycles, 2-cycle recovery) would remove family 1 but
leave Fmax pinned by the ALU paths, and it gives up about 1.5% IPC
against 1-cycle recovery. So the best predictor-only move on this core
is the 1-cycle-recovery predictor. It measured 4,201,740 cycles (-6.46%,
+6.9% iter/cycle) and was Fmax-neutral on the 001-r2s0 base (003-r3s2:
58.87 vs 57.82 MHz, +8.85% fitness). LESSONS.md calls it a stackable,
Fmax-neutral ~7-9% IPC win to re-apply on the current champion. It does
not overlap with 001-r3s0's operand-path fixes.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Port the 003-r3s2 predictor onto the current RTL, which already has the
LUT-RAM regfile, ID-precomputed one-hot forward selects and the syn_keep
result OR. The redirect's late-compare depth must stay at or below the
champion's.

Fetch (if_stage.sv):
  * bht: 64 x 2-bit saturating counters in flops (reset 2'b01). Read index
    is pc[7:2], straight off the PC register.
  * Predecode the raw same-cycle imem_data (a registered LFSR in the timed
    bench, so reg-to-reg):
      f_jal = opcode==1101111
      f_br  = opcode==1100011 && funct3 not in {2,3}
      f_imm = instr[3] ? J-imm : B-imm
      f_tgt = pc + f_imm
    pred_taken = (f_jal || (f_br && bht_rd[1])) && !f_imm[1]. A misaligned
    target is never predicted, so the misalign-trap path is unchanged.
  * PC priority: reset > redirect ? redirect_target > stall hold >
    pred_taken ? f_tgt : pc+4. Redirect stays the last select, so the late
    signal still enters the PC D through one mux. The PC takes the
    predicted path exactly when ID/EX captures a valid instruction
    (!stall_if && !redirect  <=>  !stall_id && !flush_id). So the
    pred_taken latched with an instruction is always the one that steered
    the PC.
  * Export pred_taken and bht_ctr[1:0] in if_id_t. out.instr stays the raw
    imem word (no NOP mux).
  * BHT write port driven only from EX/MEM flops: en = ex_mem.valid &&
    ex_mem.ctrl.is_branch, idx = ex_mem.pc[7:2], taken =
    ex_mem.branch_taken, new = sat(ex_mem.bht_ctr, taken). A branch sits
    in EX/MEM for exactly one cycle (dmem_stall needs a mem op there), so
    it updates exactly once. The EX compare must not fan out to BHT
    enables.

ID (id_stage.sv): latch pred_taken and bht_ctr as plain CE=!stall data
flops (not in the sync-cleared kill group), so the flush fanout stays at
6 flops. They are only consumed through is_branch/is_jump, which are
already cleared on bubbles.

EX (ex_stage.sv), mispredict-only redirect with no added levels:
  * redirect = pred_taken_q ? (is_branch && !branch_cond)
                            : ((branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault)
    Only branch_cond is late. pred_taken_q is a flop select, so the
    compare -> redirect depth equals today's. A predicted JAL never

title: Pre-decode EX control into ID/EX flops and collapse the result tail to one LUT (gated DSP input)
motivation:
`python3 -m tools.eval.gowin bench --all-options` on the champion
(002-r4s1) gives p1 = p2 = 90.209 MHz, so the median is set by p1/p2,
not by the p0 path stored in log.jsonl. In p1, 25 paths are tied
within 0.3 ns (16.10-16.38 ns arrival, period 11.09 ns). They form
four families, and each has a cheap control-side prefix or suffix:
 1. alu_op_3 -> u_alu/sub_s2 -> sub_s4 -> n12_s3 -> 32-cell add33 carry
    chain -> res_early_31 (4 LUTs) -> res_mid_31 -> ex_result_31
    (paths 1,3,4; 16.38 ns). Decoding `sub = (op == ALU_SUB)` from the
    5-bit flop op costs 2 LUT levels plus routing = 1.95 ns
    (5.56 -> 7.52) before the adder even starts.
 2. EX/MEM.alu_result / fwd1_exmem -> rs1 forward LUT -> shifter ->
    res_early (4-6 LUTs) -> res_mid -> ex_result (paths 2,5,6,13-15,
    20-22; 16.1-16.37 ns). rs1 -> first shifter LUT is a 2.6-3.2 ns
    high-fanout route.
 3. EX/MEM.alu_result -> rs2 forward -> 17-cell compare chain ->
    u_if/n328 (4 LUT levels: case(branch_op), is_branch, misalign
    check that itself re-uses branch_cond, redirect) -> u_id/n778
    flush -> ID/EX kill flops and PC (paths 7-12,16-19,24,25; 16.29).

    16.12 ns).

LUT2 levels res_mid = res_early | mul_lo and ex_result = res_mid |
mul_hi. That is about 0.9 ns of LUT + route that only exists so the
DSP can enter last.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Four cycle-exact micro-optimizations that remove 1-2 LUT levels from
every tied family. CoreMark cycles stay at 4.49M:
A. ALU sub-selects pre-decoded in ID and registered in ID/EX as plain
   CE=!stall data flops: alu_sub, alu_sra, cmp_signed (SLT/SLTI or
   BLT/BGE), and split RS_LOGIC into one-hot RS_AND/RS_OR/RS_XOR
   result classes. alu.sv then has no `op ==` compare on the data
   path. `sub` becomes a flop that merges into the rs2 forward LUT
   (fwd2, exmem[i], rs2_val[i], sub = LUT4), which removes about
   1.9 ns from family 1.
B. The result tail becomes one LUT. Add an ID/EX flop is_mul
   (MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU) and a flop mul_hi_sel, plus mul_a_signed /
   mul_b_signed flops for the DSP sign bits. Feed the DSP a separate,
   syn_keep'd operand copy a_dsp = is_mul ? rs1 : 0, so it is one
   LUT4 (is_mul, fwd1, exmem[i], rs1_val[i]). This copy also takes
   the DSP load off the shared rs1 net. With a_dsp = 0 the whole
   product is 0 for non-multiply ops, so no sel gating is needed after
   the DSP:
     ex_result = res_early | (mul_hi_sel ? prod[63:32] : prod[31:0])
   This is a single LUT4 after both res_early (syn_keep) and the DSP.
   Delete res_mid. The DSP path then drops from 2 LUTs to 1 after the
   product, and every non-DSP path loses one LUT level (about
   0.6-0.9 ns). Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS keep the explicit
   sel-gated stand-ins (formal only, not timed).
C. Branch/redirect pre-decode. In ID, compute the branch/JAL target
   low bits (pc[1:0] + imm[1:0]) and register data flops br_eq, br_ne,
   br_lt (BLT|BLTU), br_ge (BGE|BGEU), each already ANDed with
   "target aligned", plus jal_ok (JAL and target aligned) and is_jalr.
   is_branch_q and is_jump_q remain the only flush-cleared kill bits,
   so the redirect/flush fanout does not grow. In EX, use one shared
   33-bit compare lt = {cmp_signed&rs1[31],rs1} < {cmp_signed&rs2[31],
   rs2}. It serves both SLT/SLTI (rs2 already carries the folded
   immediate) and branches, which takes one carry chain and its rs1/rs2
   loads off the critical nets. The redirect becomes:

     t_lt = is_branch_q & (lt ? br_lt : br_ge)          // LUT4

   misalign logic, but they feed only RVFI and are pruned. The
   reg_write gate uses jal_ok / addr_sum[1] only.

   compare, and give the shifter its own syn_keep'd copy
   rs1_sh/shamt. This cuts the 2.6-3.2 ns fanout route at the head of
   family 2. If Gowin merges the copies, drop D and keep A-C.

arrival (period about 9.9-10.2 ns, 98-101 MHz), roughly +8-11% Fmax
at unchanged IPC. Cost: about 15 extra FF and about 60-100 LUTs for the
duplicated forward muxes.

title: Split the 33x33 multiply across EX and MEM: register the raw DSP product in EX/MEM, select lo/hi in MEM's wb_next, MUL interlocks like a load
motivation:
After 002-r4s1 cut the shared operand-bypass prefix, the champion's
reported critical path (seed p0, 77.0 MHz, slack -7.986 ns at the
5 ns constraint, 14 logic levels, 36 cells) is
  ID/EX.ctrl.alu_op[4] -> op==MULH/MULHSU compare -> a_sx/b_sx
  -> 33x33 signed DSP product (2 DSP blocks + ALU54 combine)
  -> prod[63:32] -> sel & mul_hi -> res_mid | mul_hi -> EX/MEM.alu_result[31].
So the DSP is now on the critical path. The 002-r1s1 lesson ("keep
MUL single-cycle unless make timing names the DSP path") no longer
applies: timing now names it. The multiply is also the only EX
producer that cannot be shortened with LUT-level tricks. A 33x33
product made from 18x18 tiles needs a partial-product combine after
the multipliers, and today that combine, the result OR and the
EX/MEM setup all happen in the same cycle as the 2:1 forward mux and
the signedness decode that feed the DSP.
The IPC cost of moving the multiply result one stage later is tiny.
CoreMark's MULs are in the matrix kernels (about 2*N^3 + 2*N^2 with
N about 9, so roughly 1.6-2.2k per iteration against 449k cycles per
iteration). Even if every MUL is followed by a dependent instruction,
the extra interlock bubble costs at most about 0.5% of cycles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Change where the multiply result is produced. Today it is an
EX-stage result class. After this change it is a MEM-stage result,
like a load. The DSP spans the EX -> MEM boundary and never sits in
the EX result tree.
1. Signedness is pre-decoded in ID. The decoder emits mul_a_signed
   (MULH, MULHSU) and mul_b_signed (MULH), and ID/EX registers them.
   EX computes a_sx = rs1[31] & mul_a_signed_q and
   b_sx = rs2[31] & mul_b_signed_q. The 5-bit alu_op compare leaves
   the path into the DSP, so the DSP inputs are one 2:1 forward LUT
   of flops plus one AND for the sign bit.
2. The raw product is registered in EX/MEM. EX computes
   prod = a_ext * b_ext and registers prod[63:0] (or its ALTOPS
   stand-ins v_mullo/v_mulhi) in new EX/MEM fields mul_lo_q and
   mul_hi_q, under the same CE (= !stall) as the rest of data_q.
   Synthesis can then absorb the register into the DSP output
   register or retime the partial-product combine across it. The
   alu.sv exports mul_lo/mul_hi are removed from ex_result. The EX
   result becomes early | LINK | DIV, and the syn_keep res_mid split
   is no longer needed.
3. The lo/hi select happens in MEM. EX/MEM carries registered
   one-hot bits is_mullo and is_mulhi, copied from ID/EX
   res_sel[RS_MULLO] and res_sel[RS_MULHI]. mem_stage forms
   nonload = is_mullo ? mul_lo_q : is_mulhi ? mul_hi_q : alu_result
   from flops only, then wb_next = mem_to_reg ? load_data : nonload.
   The late BSRAM load data therefore enters only the final 2:1 LUT,
   exactly as today. wb_next already feeds MEM/WB.wdata and the ID
   capture bypass, so the distance-2 consumer gets the product with
   no new forwarding path.
4. Distance-1 MUL consumers interlock like load-use. ID/EX registers
   late_result = mem_read | is_mul (is_mul = res_sel MULLO or MULHI).
   hazard_unit's load-use term uses late_result in place of
   id_ex_mem_read, so a dependent instruction right behind a MUL
   gets one bubble and then captures the product through the
   existing fwd?_mem ID-capture path. EX/MEM.alu_result is never
   selected as a MUL source: after the bubble the MUL sits in MEM,
   not EX/MEM->EX. Stores that use a MUL result as data are covered
   the same way, because the hazard compares rs2 too.
5. Flatten redirect, the tied second family. A fresh `make timing`
   on the champion (seed p0) shows paths 2-5 at 18.272 ns, within
   0.01 ns of the DSP path (18.281 ns):
     ID/EX.fwd1_exmem -> rs1 2:1 mux -> 32-bit compare carry chain
     -> 1.9 ns net -> 4 LUT levels in the redirect decode
     (branch_op case select, is_branch/is_jump, misalign_branch,
     misalign_jump) -> redirect (fanout 34: PC mux + flush) -> ID
     flush LUT -> RESET of the ID/EX kill bits.
   Pipelining the MUL alone would leave this family setting Fmax,
   so the same change shortens it. In ID, pre-decode one-hot
   registered branch kinds br_eq, br_ne, br_lt, br_ge, br_ltu and
   br_geu. Each is already ANDed with "target aligned", computed
   in ID from flops only: B/J-imm targets are pc + imm with

title: Low-area bimodal+JAL fetch predictor: LUT-RAM BHT, flop-selected redirect precomputed in ID, on the 90 MHz champion
motivation:
A Python-ISS trace of coremark.elf (2.94M instructions) shows 296k taken
branches, 49.6k JALs and 13.8k JALRs. Each costs one flushed fetch slot on
the champion (002-r4s1, 90.2 MHz, 4.49M cycles), about 8% of all cycles.
In the same trace, a 64-entry 2-bit bimodal plus always-taken JAL nets
293k saved cycles (275.8k taken-and-predicted + 49.6k JAL - 32.1k
wrong-taken). That matches the 4.20M cycles that 003-r1s2 and 003-r4s2
measured, which is +7.0% IPC. Static BTFN would net only 234k (52k
loop-exit mispredicts), which is too close to the 4.6% acceptance bar.
003-r4s2 lost about 7% Fmax on 001-r3s0 even though its worst path
stayed the existing ALU path. Likely causes: +430 LUT / +177 FF (a
64x2 flop BHT with a 64:1 fabric read mux) disturbing placement, and a
5-input redirect term added to the branch-compare->redirect->flush
family. 001-r3s0 shows that family ends at ID/EX valid_q.

Keep the measured bimodal+JAL predictor (1-cycle recovery) but shrink
it and keep it off the champion's timing families.
(1) The BHT is 64x2 in async distributed LUT-RAM, mapped the same way as
the regfile: syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram" with an initial fill of
2'b01 and no reset. It is read at pc[7:2] straight from the PC flops

!stall_ex_mem, saturating counter carried from fetch). This removes
about 128 FF and the 64:1 mux.

f_imm = instr[3] ? J-imm : B-imm, f_tgt = pc + f_imm, and
pred = (f_jal | f_br & ctr[1]) & ~f_imm[1]. Next-PC priority is
redirect > stall hold > pred ? f_tgt : pc+4.

flush): rd_t = !pred & !imm[1] & (is_branch | is_jal), and

branch_taken & !misalign. redirect_target = is_jalr ? jalr_tgt :
(pred & is_branch) ? pc+4 : pc+imm, so the target mux is selected only
by flops.

fitness, for about +100 LUT / +10 FF.

title: Register the redirect decision (EX kill flop + late-select fetch PC) and put the ALU adder at the last LUT of the EX result
motivation:
A fresh `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (002-r5s1, seed p0,
93.7 MHz, 11 levels) shows two path families tied within 0.04 ns.
The fix must cut both (lessons 002-r3s1 and 001-r4s0).

Family 1 (paths 1-3 and 5-25, data delay 10.64 ns). The path is
  ID/EX.fwd1_exmem (fanout 35, 1.43 ns net) -> rs1 fwd LUT (fanout 14,
  1.15 ns) -> 32-bit compare carry chain (ends at 9.97)
  -> 1.53 ns net -> 4 LUTs in u_if (redirect AND-OR merged with the
  stall term, n328_s20/s10/s4/s0) -> fanout-34 net (0.77)
  -> pc_30_s3 LUT (fanout 30) -> 0.95 ns net -> the CE pin of all 32 PC
  flops.
After the compare there are about 6 ns of logic, and about 2.4 ns of it
exists only to get the late redirect onto the D and CE pins of the
32-bit PC. Separately, redirect also drives flush_id into the ID/EX
kill-bit flops.

Family 2 (path 4, data delay 10.60 ns). The path is
  ID/EX.ctrl.alu_op[0] -> sub decode (2 LUTs, 1.96 ns including net)
  -> b^sub -> add33 carry chain (SUM at 11.15)
  -> 6 LUT levels (ex_result_16_s9/s8/s6/s11/s1/s0, 4.78 ns)
  -> EX/MEM.alu_result.
The adder, the latest-arriving class, enters the head of a 6-deep
AND-OR. Lesson 001-r3s0 fixed the same problem for the DSP with a
syn_keep split, but that fix was lost when the multiply moved to MEM.
alu_op is also still decoded in EX to get `sub`.

Both fixes are cycle-exact: the redirect still takes effect on the
very next fetch, and nothing moves to a later stage. So IPC stays at
4.53M cycles and the full Fmax gain goes to fitness.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Part A: register the redirect decision (drop redirect's fanout from
about 50 pins to 1 flop).
1. ex_stage adds one resettable flop, kill_q:
     kill_q <= redirect & ~stall_id
   where redirect is the existing flat AND-OR now gated by ~kill_q.
   While a branch or jump is in EX, load_use and div_stall are 0, so
   in practice this is redirect & ~dmem_stall. kill_q = 1 means that
   the instruction now in ID/EX is wrong-path. It is the word ID/EX
   captured on the redirect edge, which is no longer flushed.
2. kill_q kills that instruction in EX instead of flushing it into
   ID/EX. It gates:
     - EX/MEM valid_q, reg_write_q, mem_read_q and mem_write_q, at
       their D inputs;
     - wen_next, so the ID forward precompute does not forward from it;
     - late_result into hazard_unit, as late_eff = late_result_q &
       ~kill_q, computed from two flops in parallel with the
       rd==rs compare;
     - is_div, so the divider never starts on it;
     - redirect itself.
   At t+1, stall_id is always 0 (EX/MEM holds the branch, which has no
   memory op, and load_use and div_stall are gated). So kill_q never
   needs a hold term. The implementer should keep
   `| (kill_q & stall_id)` anyway if formal wants it.
3. hazard_unit: remove redirect from flush_id. It becomes
     !dmem_stall && !div_stall && (load_use || imem_stall).
   Remove redirect from stall/priority logic too.
4. if_stage: late-select fetch PC. Replace the single PC flop with:
     - pc_seq, the sequential PC;
     - pc_tgt <= redirect_target, captured every cycle with no enable;
     - the architectural fetch address
         fetch_pc = kill_q ? pc_tgt : pc_seq
       (one LUT from flops), which drives io_imemAddr and the IF/ID pc.
   The next pc_seq is
     kill_q ? (stall_if ? pc_tgt : pc_tgt+4) : (stall_if ? pc_seq : pc_seq+4)
   with both +4 adders fed from flops. `redirect` no longer reaches any
   PC D or CE pin. Only kill_q does, and it is a flop.
5. Cycle equivalence with today:
   - Taken branch at t: the target is fetched at t+1 and one slot is
     killed, the same as the flush today.
   - Redirect under dmem stall: the branch is held. Today the PC is
     re-pointed and the word is flushed on the release edge. The new
     scheme fetches the target on the cycle after release, which is
     the same cycle as today.
   - imem stall at t+1: pc_seq takes pc_tgt and fetch retries it.
   - Misaligned targets never redirect (the existing kill bits), so
     the trap and pc_next logic is unchanged.
   - RVFI is unchanged, because killed instructions never retire.
Expected effect on family 1: it ends at kill_q.D, which is about 2-3
LUTs after the compare. That removes the fanout-34 and fanout-30 nets
and one LUT, about 2 ns, so the path lands at about 8.6 ns.

Part B: put the adder at the last LUT of the EX result and pre-decode
the ALU sub-selects. This is the stackable part A of lesson 001-r5s0,
plus the syn_keep split from 001-r3s0.
6. The decoder and ID/EX register one-hot sub-selects as plain CE flops:
     alu_sub (ALU_SUB), alu_sra (ALU_SRA), slt_signed (ALU_SLT),
     log_and and log_or (XOR is the default).
   alu.sv uses these flops instead of `op ==` compares, so there are

title: Capture-side distance-1 bypass: resolve the EX->EX forward at the ID/EX D input so every EX operand is a bare flop
motivation:
The champion (002-r5s1, 99.76 MHz median, 4.53M cycles) is limited by the
EX path family: the scored worst path starts at the registered select
ID/EX.fwd1_exmem (fanout 32 to the per-bit forward LUTs), goes through
the 2:1 EX/MEM->EX forward mux, the 32-bit compare, the flat redirect
AND-OR and ends on the PC flops (11 levels, 34 cells). The same forward
mux is the head of every other EX family: ALU adder/shifter/SLT -> result
AND-OR -> EX/MEM.alu_result, rs1+imm address adder -> dmem BSRAM address,
DSP operand inputs, and the JALR target -> PC. 002-r4s1 got +9.4% by
moving the distance-2 bypass and the immediate into the ID/EX capture;
001-r4s0 showed that any select left in front of the EX operands stays in
the critical tie. The last select left in EX is the distance-1 bypass.
No prior hypothesis in log.jsonl has moved it.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move the distance-1 (EX -> next instruction) bypass from the head of EX to
the tail of EX, in the ID/EX D input. The instruction in ID captures the
result that the instruction in EX computes in the same cycle, so at the
next edge rs1_val/rs2_val already hold the final operand. EX's rs1/rs2
become the ID/EX flops with no mux, and EX/MEM.alu_result is no longer a
forward source; it only feeds MEM's wb_next and RVFI.

The change is cycle-exact: the same forwarding cases, the same load-use
and mul-use interlocks, and no new stalls.
- Distance 1 (writer in EX): new capture term. fwd?_ex = ex_wen_next &&
  ID/EX.rd != 0 && rd == instr rs?. These are the same compares
  id_stage already computes for fwd?_exmem, now used at capture instead
  of registered.
- Distance 2 (writer in MEM): unchanged wb_next capture.
- Distance 3: unchanged regfile write-first bypass.
- LOAD/MUL in EX (late_result): the existing load-use interlock prevents
  the dependent capture, as it does today.
- DIV: ID/EX holds during div_stall. On the done cycle ex_result
  carries div_result (a flop), so the consumer captures it.
- dmem stall: ID/EX and EX/MEM both hold, the EX instruction's operands
  are held flops, and the consumer captures after the stall releases, as
  it does today.

Keep the ALU tail from gaining a LUT level. Do not build
`fwd?_ex ? ex_result : other` after the full result OR. Instead, gate
each result class with a capture select that is precomputed early:
g1_k = fwd1_ex & ID/EX.res_sel[k], and similarly g2_k with the
!imm_operand gate. fwd?_ex comes from the flop-driven imem word compared
with the ID/EX.rd flop in about 3 LUTs, and res_sel is a flop, so both
are ready long before the ALU. The captured value is
rs1_d = OR_k(g1_k & v_k) | (~fwd1_ex & (fwd1_mem ? wb_next : rs1_data)),
which has the same AND-OR depth as ex_result itself.

Fold the flop-only classes (LINK = pc+4, PASSB = folded imm, DIV = div
res_q) into one "misc" value computed from flops. The late per-class
terms are then only ADD, LOGIC, SLL, SR and SLT, in both the EX/MEM
result OR and the two capture ORs. Load data still enters only the last
LUT of the capture.

Expected effect: every EX path family loses its first LUT and the
fanout-32 route from the select flop, about 1.2-1.8 ns of the ~10 ns
period. The redirect->PC, address-adder->BSRAM, DSP-input and
JALR-target families gain it all. The ALU->operand loop keeps its depth
but loses the head LUT. Per the LESSONS rule for many tied families,
count on about half of that saving: roughly +7-9% median Fmax at an
unchanged 4.53M cycles. The cost is about +300-500 LUT4 for the two
duplicated class AND-ORs (area is 2.3k of a 10k budget).

title: PC-indexed LUT-RAM BTB with registered (2-cycle) mispredict recovery: take branch-compare->PC off the critical path
motivation:
On the 002-r5s1 champion (99.76 MHz, ~4.53M cycles) `make timing` names
clock -> cpu/u_ex -> cpu/u_if as the worst path: the branch compare ->
flat redirect AND-OR -> 32-bit PC mux (plus flush fanout) is the cycle
limiter. Every earlier predictor (003-r1s2 .. 003-r5s2) kept this
same-cycle EX->PC redirect and added a second, imem_data-dependent
predecode -> pc+imm -> PC loop, so they gained ~7% IPC but lost it again
in Fmax (LESSONS 003-r4s2, 003-r5s2: "on a core whose redirect->PC path
is in the critical tie, 1-cycle-recovery prediction cannot pay"). The
lesson's suggested alternative is registered 2-cycle recovery (003-r2s2
measured 4.27M cycles with it even without JALR prediction). The missing
piece is a fetch-side predictor that does NOT depend on imem_data: a
BTB indexed by the PC flop makes the next-fetch-PC loop
PC -> LUT-RAM -> tag compare -> 2:1 mux -> PC, all flop-sourced, and
lets EX resolve the branch into a flop instead of into the PC.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the same-cycle EX redirect with a PC-indexed branch target buffer
in IF and a registered mispredict that recovers the PC from EX/MEM one
cycle later.

(1) Fetch (if_stage / new rtl/btb.sv). 64-entry direct-mapped BTB in async
LUT-RAM (syn_ramstyle="distributed_ram", `initial` zero fill, NO reset —
LESSONS r3s0), index pc[7:2], partial tag pc[13:8] + valid, 30-bit
target[31:2]; a separate 64x2 LUT-RAM holds a 2-bit saturating counter
(split so a not-taken update rewrites only the counter and keeps the
target). pred_taken = valid & tag_hit & ctr[1]. Next PC:
  mispredict_q ? EX/MEM.pc_next          (flop, overrides every stall)
  : stall_if   ? pc
  : pred_taken ? {btb_target, 2'b00} : pc + 4.
Nothing in this loop reads imem_data or any EX signal. pred_taken,
pred_target and the read counter travel with the instruction into ID/EX
(pred_taken in the reset/flush-cleared kill group so bubbles never
"predict").

(2) EX verify, registered. The existing flat `redirect` AND-OR (actual
taken & aligned) is kept but now only feeds a flop:
  tgt_match = is_jalr_k ? (rs1 == jalr_d_q)            // jalr_d = pred_target - imm, precomputed in ID
                        : (branch_target[31:2] == pred_target_q) // flop-only pc+imm adder
  mis = valid & !mispredict_q & (pred_taken_q ? !(redirect & tgt_match) : redirect)
registered as EX/MEM.mispredict_q (CE = !stall_ex_mem). Both target
compares run in parallel with the three branch compares, so the D input
of mispredict_q is about one LUT deeper than today's redirect but drives
one flop instead of the 32-bit PC mux + flush fanout. The recovery target
is the already-registered EX/MEM.pc_next (actual next PC incl. misalign
trap -> pc+4), so correctness never depends on BTB contents (formal's
symbolic imem can change the word at a PC: any wrong target, aliasing or
non-branch hit is simply a mispredict).

(3) Squash on mispredict_q (all flop-sourced): hazard_unit's `redirect`
input becomes mispredict_q (flush_id clears the IF/ID word); ex_stage
ANDs !mispredict_q into the EX/MEM valid/reg_write/mem_read/mem_write
captures, into is_div (no divider start, no div_stall on a wrong-path
DIV) and into mis itself, killing the wrong-path instruction already in
ID/EX. dmem_stall cannot coincide (EX/MEM holds the branch, not a memory
op).

(4) BTB update from EX/MEM flops only (write next cycle): on a valid
taken branch/JAL/JALR write tag/target = pc_next[31:2] and ctr =
sat_inc(ctr_q) (allocate as 2'b10 on a miss); on a valid not-taken
branch that hit, write ctr = sat_dec(ctr_q) to the counter RAM only.

Cycle model (ISS trace from 003-r5s2: 296k taken branches, 49.6k JAL,
13.8k JALR per run): correctly predicted taken B/JAL/JALR now cost 0
bubbles (today 1), correct not-taken 0, a mispredict 2. 003-r2s2
measured exactly this recovery scheme at 4.266M cycles against a 4.49M
base (-224k, JALR never predicted). The champion is at 4.528M (MUL
interlock), so expect ~4.30M; BTB-predicted JALR (single-caller returns,
function-pointer calls) wins back up to ~20k, 64-entry cold/alias misses
cost some of that, net ~4.29-4.32M (-4.6 to -5.3% cycles). Fmax: the
named worst path disappears;
the new fetch loop is ~LUT-RAM + 2 LUT tag compare + fanout + 1 mux
(est. 6-7 ns), mispredict_q's D is compare + 3 LUTs into one flop. If
the next family (ALU / load->ID capture) sits at 102-105 MHz, fitness
gains ~+7-10%; at unchanged Fmax the IPC alone lands right at the 4.6%
bar, so the win depends on Fmax not falling.

Implementation guards: (a) correctness never trusts the BTB — tgt_match
compares against the real pc+imm / rs1, and the JALR check rs1==jalr_d
is exact (an odd rs1+imm just mispredicts and recovers to pc_next);
(b) if the jalr_d subtract in ID shows in `make timing`, compare
addr_sum[31:2]==pred_target_q in EX instead; (c) if the BTB read ->
tag -> PC loop is in the top paths, drop to 32 entries (index pc[6:2],

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r6s2 (regression, +0.22%): A PC-indexed 64-entry LUT-RAM BTB with registered 2-cycle mispredict recovery (the fix the 003-r5s2 lesson suggested) scored 220.83 vs 220.34, which implies median Fmax fell to about 95 MHz at the modeled ~4.30M cycles (at most 100 MHz even if cycles did not drop), while sibling 001-r6s0 registered the same EX redirect cycle-exactly (one kill_q flop, fetch PC late-selected from flops) with no predictor and reached 111.5 MHz, so the predictor's own logic, not the redirect, cost at least 10% Fmax (likely the new PC -> LUT-RAM bank read -> tag compare -> pred_taken -> 4-arm next-PC mux fetch loop, and a mispredict D input made deeper by the 30-bit pc+imm target compare, the 32-bit rs1==jalr_d compare and the pred_taken/div_stall gating); because a predictor removes only ~5% of cycles here, it pays only if both its fetch loop and its verify logic stay under 001-r6s0's ~9 ns kill_q path on every placement seed, so time a prototype before spending another round on predictors.
